header.title: Commedia I: Inferno: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Dante Alighieri
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's urn:dante:commedia:inferno:petrocchi, from UD Italian-Old: Petrocchi's text via DanteSearch (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. Only some passages are translated so far: those that the Atlas of Ancient Myth, Magic in the Ancient Texts and the demons-and-angels study cite.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
header.availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit UD Italian-Old: Petrocchi's text via DanteSearch and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

notes.14.44: 14.80: 'peccatrici', sinful women, probably prostitutes; some editions read 'pettatrici' (hemp-combers).
notes.20.29: 20.30: the sense of 'passion comporta' is disputed: to feel grief or pity at God's judgment, or to bring one's own feeling to bear on it. 20.64–66: the construction is uncertain, and 'Pennino' may be the Pennine Alps or a particular peak.
notes.20.104: 20.124–125: the subject of 'holds' and 'touches' is Cain with his thorns (the moon), named in the line after the unit.
notes.26.88: 26.141 "com'altrui piacque", literally "as pleased another": Ulysses does not name God, and the English keeps the indirection.
notes.4.84: 4.95 "quel segnor de l'altissimo canto" is usually taken to be Homer; some take it as Virgil.
notes.31.14: 31.14 is compressed: taken as Dante tracing the sound back along its path toward its source. 31.17 "la santa gesta": the holy band of paladins; some read "the holy enterprise".
notes.16.135: 17.16 "sommesse e sovraposte": taken as the ground and the raised pattern of woven cloth; the exact technical sense is uncertain.
notes.25.15: 25.18 "l'acerbo", literally "the unripe one": taken as "the harsh" or "the insolent one"; the sense is debated.
notes.31.110: 31.110 "dotta" taken as "fear"; some read it as "moment". 31.123 can also be construed "where Cocytus locks in the cold".
notes.11.50: 11.50: Cahors stands for usury. 11.54 'fidanza non imborsa', literally 'does not purse up trust', is taken as one who has placed no special trust in the deceiver.
notes.27.110: 27.127 'foco furo': the 'thieving' fire, which hides the sinner inside it.
notes.3.35: 3.42: the sense of 'alcuna gloria ... d'elli' is disputed; taken here as the damned having some glory over them.
notes.17.95: 17.95 'ad altro forse': 'forse' is taken as a noun, 'peril' or 'doubt'; the phrase is disputed.
notes.18.135: 19.6-7: 'bolgia' (pouch) and 'tomba' (tomb) are Dante's names for the ditches of this circle.
notes.21.27: 21.38: Saint Zita stands for Lucca, whose 'elders' (anziani) were magistrates; 21.48-49: the Holy Face is Lucca's crucifix, the Serchio its river. 21.46 'convolto' may mean 'doubled over' or 'covered over' (with pitch).
notes.21.74: 21.78 'Che li approda?' is obscure; taken as 'what good will it do him?'. 21.95: Caprona is a castle whose garrison surrendered under terms. 21.124 'pane' is taken as birdlime, that is, the pitch.
notes.31.65: 31.67 is meaningless speech by design and is left untranslated.

nodes.text: Halfway along the road of our life
I found myself in a dark forest,
for the straight way had been lost.
Ah, how hard a thing it is to tell what it was like,
this wood, wild and harsh and dense,
“Have mercy on me,” I cried to him,
“whatever you are, a shade or a real man!”
He answered me: “Not a man; a man I was once,
and my parents were Lombards,
both of them Mantuans by their homeland.
I was born under Julius, though it was late,
and I lived at Rome under the good Augustus
in the time of the false and lying gods.
I was a poet, and I sang of that just
son of Anchises who came from Troy
after proud Ilium was burned.
But you, why are you going back to such misery?
Why do you not climb the delightful mountain
until he has put her back in Hell,
from where envy first sent her out.
So I think and judge, for your good,
that you should follow me, and I will be your guide,
and I will lead you from here through an eternal place,
where you will hear the despairing shrieks,
you will see the ancient spirits in pain,
So I said to him; and when he had moved on,
I entered on the deep and wooded road.
"Through me one goes into the grieving city,
through me one goes into eternal pain,
through me one goes among the lost people.
Justice moved my high maker;
divine power made me,
the highest wisdom and the first love.
Before me no things were created
except eternal ones, and I endure eternally.
Leave every hope behind, you who enter."
These words, dark in colour,
I saw written at the top of a gate;
is kept by the sad souls of those
who lived without disgrace and without praise.
They are mixed in with that worthless choir
of the angels who were not rebels
nor were faithful to God, but were for themselves.
The heavens drive them out so as not to be less fair,
nor does deep Hell receive them,
for the guilty would have some glory from them.”
And I: “Master, what is so heavy
upon them that it makes them wail so loud?”
fearing that my talk might weigh on him,
I kept from speaking until we reached the river.
And look, coming toward us in a boat,
an old man, white with ancient hair,
shouting: "Woe to you, wicked souls!
Never hope to see the sky:
I come to take you to the other bank,
into the eternal darkness, into heat and frost.
And you there, living soul,
get away from these who are dead."
But when he saw that I was not leaving,
he said: "By another way, by other ports
you will come to shore, not here, to cross:
a lighter boat must carry you."
And the guide to him: "Charon, do not rage:
it is willed so there where one can do
what one wills, and ask no more."
At this the woolly cheeks fell quiet
of the pilot of the livid marsh,
who had wheels of flame around his eyes.
But those souls, who were weary and naked,
changed colour and clattered their teeth,
as soon as they heard the cruel words.
They cursed God and their parents,
the human race, and the place and the time and the seed
of their begetting and of their births.
Then they drew back, all of them together,
weeping loudly, to the evil shore
that waits for every man who does not fear God.
Charon the demon, with eyes like embers,
beckoning to them, gathers them all in;
he strikes with his oar any that lags.
As in autumn the leaves lift away
one after another, until the branch
they had a look neither sad nor glad.
The good master began to say:
"Look at that one with the sword in his hand,
who comes in front of the three as their lord:
that is Homer, sovereign poet;
the next who comes is Horace the satirist;
Ovid is the third, and the last is Lucan.
Because each of them shares with me
the name that the single voice sounded,
they do me honour, and in that they do well."
So I saw gathered the fair school
of that lord of the loftiest song
who flies above the others like an eagle.
When they had talked together for a while,
they turned to me with a sign of greeting,
and my master smiled at this;
and they did me far more honour still,
for they made me one of their company,
so that I was sixth among so much wisdom.
So we went on as far as the light,
speaking of things about which it is good to keep silent,
just as speaking was [good], there where I was.
We came to the foot of a noble castle,
circled seven times by high walls,
defended all around by a fair little stream.
This we crossed as if it were solid ground;
through seven gates I went in with these sages:
we came to a meadow of fresh green.
There were people there with slow and serious eyes,
of great authority in their looks:
they spoke seldom, with gentle voices.
So we drew aside to one of the edges,
into an open place, full of light, and high,
so that all of them could be seen.
There, straight before me, on the green enamel,
the great spirits were shown to me,
and for having seen them I exult within myself.
I saw Electra with many companions,
among whom I knew Hector and Aeneas,
Caesar in armour, with a hawk's eyes.
I saw Camilla and Penthesilea;
on the other side I saw King Latinus,
who sat with Lavinia his daughter.
I saw that Brutus who drove out Tarquin,
Lucretia, Julia, Marcia and Cornelia;
and alone, set apart, I saw Saladin.
When I raised my brows a little higher,
I saw the master of those who know
down into the second, which girds less space
and so much more pain, which goads to wailing.
There Minos stands, hideous, and snarls:
he examines the sins at the entrance;
he judges and sends down according to how he coils.
I mean that when the ill-born soul
comes before him, it confesses everything;
and that examiner of sins
sees which place in hell belongs to it;
he wraps his tail around himself as many times
as the levels he wills that it be sent down.
Always before him many of them stand:
they go in turn, each one, to the judgment,
that she made whatever pleased lawful by her law,
to take away the blame she had incurred.
She is Semiramis, of whom we read
that she succeeded Ninus and was his wife:
she held the land the Sultan rules.
The next is she who killed herself for love
and broke faith with the ashes of Sychaeus;
then there is lustful Cleopatra.
See Helen, for whom so much evil
time rolled by, and see the great Achilles,
who fought with love at the end.
See Paris, Tristan"; and more than a thousand
shades he showed me and named, pointing with his finger,
pours down through the dark air;
the ground that receives this stinks.
Cerberus, a beast cruel and monstrous,
barks like a dog with three throats
over the people who are sunk there.
His eyes are red, his beard greasy and black,
his belly broad, and his hands clawed;
he claws the spirits, flays them and quarters them.
The rain makes them howl like dogs;
with one of their sides they shield the other;
the wretched profane ones keep turning over.
When Cerberus, the great worm, caught sight of us,
he opened his mouths and showed us his fangs;
he had no limb that he held still.
And my guide spread his hands wide,
took up earth, and with fists full
threw it into the greedy gullets.
As a dog that barks in its craving,
and grows quiet once it bites its food,
for it strains and fights only to devour it,
so did those filthy faces become
of the demon Cerberus, who so thunders at
the souls that they would wish to be deaf.
We were passing over the shades that are beaten down by
the heavy rain, and setting our soles
under the steering of a single boatman,
who was shouting: "Now you have come, wicked soul!"
"Phlegyas, Phlegyas, you shout in vain,"
said my lord, "this time:
you will not have us longer than for crossing the mud."
As one who hears of a great deceit
that has been done to him, and then resents it,
so Phlegyas became in his pent-up rage.
My guide stepped down into the boat,
and then had me go in after him;
but a wailing struck my ears,
so that I open my eyes wide and fix them ahead.
The good master said: "Now, my son,
the city named Dis is drawing near,
with its grave citizens, with its great host."
And I: "Master, already its mosques
I clearly make out there inside, in the valley,
red, as if out of fire they
had come." And he said to me: "The eternal fire
that burns them within shows them red,
as you see, in this low hell."
We came at last into the deep moats
that fortify that disconsolate city:
the walls seemed to me to be of iron.
Not without first making a wide circuit
did we come to a place where the boatman, loudly,
"Get out," shouted, "here is the entrance."
I saw more than a thousand above the gates,
rained down from heaven, who angrily
were saying: "Who is this, who without death
goes through the kingdom of the dead?"
And my wise master made a sign
that he wished to speak with them in secret.
Then they held back their great disdain a little
and said: "You come alone, and let him go
who so boldly entered into this kingdom.
Let him go back alone by the mad road:
let him try, if he knows how; for you will stay here,
who have guided him through so dark a land."
Think, reader, whether I lost heart
at the sound of the accursed words,
for I did not believe I would ever return here.
"O my dear guide, who more than seven
times have restored my safety and drawn me
out of deep peril that stood against me,
do not leave me," I said, "so undone;
and if going further is denied us,
let us retrace our footsteps together, quickly."
And that lord who had led me there
said to me: "Do not fear; for our passage
no one can take from us: by such a one it is given.
But wait for me here, and your weary spirit
comfort and feed with good hope,
for I will not leave you in the lower world."
So he goes off, and leaves me there,
the sweet father, and I remain in doubt,
for yes and no contend within my head.
I could not hear what he put to them;
but he had not stood there with them long
before each one ran back inside, racing the rest.
Those adversaries of ours shut the gates
against the chest of my lord, who stayed outside
and turned back to me with slow steps.
His eyes were on the ground and his brows shorn
of all boldness, and he said amid his sighs:
"Who has denied me the houses of pain!"
And to me he said: "You, though I am angry,
do not be dismayed, for I will win the contest,
whoever busies himself inside with the defence.
This insolence of theirs is not new;
for they used it once at a less secret gate,
which is still found without a bolt.
Over it you saw the dead writing:
and already, on this side of it, down the slope,
passing through the circles without escort,
comes one by whom the city will be opened to us."
The colour that cowardice painted on me outwardly
when I saw my guide turn back,
does it happen,” he answered me, “that any of us
makes the journey on which I am going.
It is true that I was down here once before,
conjured by that cruel Erichtho
who called the shades back to their bodies.
My flesh had been stripped of me only a little while
when she made me go in within that wall
to draw a spirit out of the circle of Judas.
That is the lowest place and the darkest,
and the farthest from the heaven that turns all things:
because my eye had drawn me wholly
toward the high tower with the glowing top,
where, in an instant, there had swiftly risen
three hellish Furies stained with blood,
who had the limbs and bearing of women,
and were girdled with bright green hydras;
little serpents and horned snakes they had for hair,
with which their savage temples were bound.
And he, who knew well the handmaids
of the queen of everlasting lament,
said to me, “Look at the fierce Erinyes.
This is Megaera on the left side;
she who weeps on the right is Alecto;
Tisiphone is in the middle”; and with that he fell silent.
Each of them was tearing her breast with her nails;
they beat themselves with their palms and cried out so loud
that I pressed close to the poet in fear.
“Let Medusa come, and so we will turn him to stone,”
they all said, looking down;
“we did wrong not to avenge the assault of Theseus.”
“Turn round and keep your eyes shut;
for if the Gorgon shows herself and you should see her,
there would be no going back up, ever.”
So said the master; and he himself
turned me round, and did not trust to my hands,
but covered my eyes with his own as well.
O you who have sound understanding,
look at the teaching that is hidden
beneath the veil of the strange verses.
And now there came across the murky waves
a crash of sound, full of terror,
of your sight across that ancient foam,
there where that fume is harshest.”
As frogs before the enemy
snake all scatter through the water
until each one squats in a heap on the ground,
I saw more than a thousand ruined souls
flee like this before one who on foot
was passing over the Styx with dry soles.
He was moving that thick air away from his face,
often waving his left hand in front of him,
and only of that vexation did he seem weary.
I saw well that he was sent from heaven,
and I turned to my master; and he made a sign
that I should keep quiet and bow to him.
Ah, how full of disdain he seemed to me!
He came to the gate, and with a little wand
he opened it, for there was nothing to hold it back.
“O you driven out of heaven, despised race,”
he began, upon the horrible threshold,
“where does this arrogance in you find its lodging?
Why do you kick against that will
whose end can never be cut short,
and which has many times increased your pain?
What use is it to butt against the fates?
Your Cerberus, if you remember well,
still bears his chin and throat stripped bare for it.”
Then he turned back along the filthy road,
and said no word to us, but had the look
of a man whom some other care grips and gnaws
than the care of the one who stands before him;
and we moved our feet toward the city,
secure after the holy words.
with its seal both Sodom and Cahors
and whoever speaks, scorning God in his heart.
Fraud, by which every conscience is bitten,
a man may use on one who trusts in him
and on one who holds no trust in store.
This latter way seems to cut
only the bond of love that nature makes;
so in the second circle there nest
hypocrisy, flatteries, and whoever deals in sorcery,
falsification, theft and simony,
panders, barratry, and suchlike filth.
By the other way that love is forgotten
which nature makes, and that which is added after,
that it would give some way down to anyone above:
such was the descent of that ravine;
and on the brink of the broken slope
the infamy of Crete lay stretched out,
that was conceived in the false cow;
and when he saw us, he bit himself,
like one whom anger breaks within.
My sage cried out toward him: "Perhaps
you think the Duke of Athens is here,
who up in the world handed you your death?
Get away, beast, for this man does not come
instructed by your sister,
when it has already received the mortal blow,
and cannot walk, but leaps this way and that,
so I saw the Minotaur do;
and that wary one cried: “Run to the passage;
while he is raging, it is good that you go down.”
we shall make to Chiron, there close by you:
your will was always so hasty, to your harm.”
Then he nudged me and said: “That is Nessus,
who died for the lovely Deianira
and himself took vengeance for himself.
And the one in the middle, who gazes at his chest,
is the great Chiron, who reared Achilles;
that other is Pholus, who was so full of rage.
Around the ditch they go in thousands upon thousands,
shooting at whatever soul pulls itself up
those wild beasts that hold in hatred
the tilled places between Cecina and Corneto.
Here the foul Harpies make their nests,
who drove the Trojans from the Strophades
with a grim announcement of harm to come.
They have broad wings, and human necks and faces,
feet with talons, and their great bellies feathered;
they make laments up in the strange trees.
And the good master: "Before you go further in,
know that you are in the second ring,"
all things except the hard-hearted demons
who came out against us at the entrance of the gate,
who is that great one who seems not to mind
the fire, and lies scornful and twisted,
so that the rain does not seem to torment him?”
And that same one, who had become aware
that I was asking my leader about him,
cried: “What I was alive, that I am dead.
Though Jove should weary his smith, from whom
in anger he took the sharp thunderbolt
with which I was struck on my last day;
or though he weary the others, by turns, one after another,
in Mongibello at the black forge,
crying, ‘Good Vulcan, help, help!’,
just as he did at the battle of Phlegra,
and hurl his bolts at me with all his strength,
he could not have a glad revenge on me.”
Then my leader spoke with a force
so great that I had never heard him so loud:
“O Capaneus, in this, that your pride
is not quenched, you are punished the more;
no torment except your own raging
would be pain fully matched to your fury.”
Then he turned back to me with a kinder look,
saying: “That was one of the seven kings
who besieged Thebes; and he held, and seems to hold,
God in disdain, and seems to prize him little;
but, as I told him, his own insults
are ornaments well fitted to his breast.
Now come behind me, and take care that you do not set
your feet, even now, on the burning sand,
but always keep your feet close in to the wood.”
In silence we came to where there spurts
out of the wood a little stream,
whose redness still makes me shudder.
As the brook that comes out of the Bulicame,
which the sinful women then share among themselves,
so this one went on down across the sand.
Its bed and both its sloping banks
were made of stone, and the edges at the side;
from which I saw that the way across was there.
“Among all the other things that I have shown you
since we entered through the gate
whose threshold is denied to no one,
nothing has been seen by your eyes
as notable as the present stream,
which quenches all the little flames above it.”
These words were my leader’s;
and so I begged him to lavish on me the food
for which he had lavished on me the hunger.
“In the middle of the sea there lies a ruined land,”
he said then, “which is called Crete,
under whose king the world was once chaste.
There is a mountain there that once was glad
with water and with leaves, which was called Ida;
now it is deserted, like a thing worn out.
Rhea once chose it as a trusty cradle
for her little son, and, to hide him better,
when he cried, she had shouts raised there.
Within the mountain a great old man stands upright,
who keeps his shoulders turned toward Damietta
and looks at Rome as at his mirror.
His head is formed of fine gold,
and pure silver are the arms and the chest;
then he is of copper down to the fork;
from there downward he is all of choice iron,
except that the right foot is baked clay,
and he stands upright on that one more than on the other.
Every part except the gold is broken
by a crack that drips tears,
which, gathered together, bore through that cave.
Their course falls from rock to rock into this valley;
they make Acheron, Styx and Phlegethon;
then they go on down by this narrow channel
until, there where there is no more descending,
they make Cocytus; and what that pool is like
you will see, so it is not told here.”
And I to him: “If the present stream
flows down in this way from our world,
this one appeared to me as I was going back into it,
and he is leading me home along this path.”
And he to me: “If you follow your star,
you cannot fail to reach a glorious harbour,
if I saw rightly in the fair life;
and if I had not died so early,
seeing heaven so kind to you,
I would have given you encouragement in your work.
But that ungrateful, malicious people
that came down from Fiesole of old,
a reef or something else hidden in the sea,
who stretches upward and draws in his feet.
"Here is the beast with the pointed tail,
that crosses mountains and breaks walls and weapons!
Here is the one that makes the whole world stink!"
So my guide began to speak to me;
and he signalled to it to come to land
near the end of the marble we had walked on.
And that filthy image of fraud
came on, and brought its head and chest ashore,
but did not draw its tail up onto the bank.
Its face was the face of a just man,
so kindly was its skin on the outside,
and all the rest of its trunk was a serpent's;
it had two paws, hairy up to the armpits;
its back and chest and both its flanks
were painted with knots and little circles.
With more colours, in ground and overlay,
Tartars or Turks never made cloth,
nor were such webs laid on the loom by Arachne.
As sometimes barges lie at the shore,
partly in the water and partly on land,
and as there among the guzzling Germans
the beaver settles itself to wage its war,
so that worst of beasts lay
on the rim that is of stone and encloses the sand.
In the void its whole tail was quivering,
twisting upward the venomous fork
that armed its tip like a scorpion's.
The guide said: "Now our way must bend
a little, as far as that
in another peril, as soon as I had mounted
clasped me with his arms and held me up;
and said: “Geryon, move now:
let your wheels be wide, and your descent slight;
think of the new load that you carry.”
toward the castle and go to Saint Peter's;
on the other side they go toward the hill.
On this side and that, along the dark rock,
I saw horned demons with great whips,
who were beating them cruelly from behind.
Ah, how they made them lift their heels
at the first strokes! Not one of them
and which the whip drives on in the same way.
And the good master, without my asking,
said to me: "Look at that great one who is coming,
who seems to shed no tears for pain:
how royal a bearing he still keeps!
That is Jason, who by courage and by wit
robbed the Colchians of the ram.
He passed by the island of Lemnos
after the bold and pitiless women
had put all their males to death.
There with tokens and with ornate words
he deceived Hypsipyle, the young girl
who had earlier deceived all the others.
He left her there, pregnant and alone;
such guilt condemns him to such torment;
and Medea too is avenged.
With him go those who deceive in that way;
and let this be enough about the first valley
great with you?’ ‘Rather, marvellous ones!’
And let our sight be satisfied with this.”
O Simon Magus, O wretched followers,
who take the things of God, which to goodness
ought to be brides, and you, rapacious,
prostitute them for gold and for silver,
now the trumpet must sound for you,
since you are in the third pouch.
We had already, at the next tomb,
climbed onto that part of the ridge
coming, silent and weeping, at the pace
that litany [processions] keep in this world.
As my gaze went lower down on them,
each one appeared, astonishingly, to be twisted
between the chin and the start of the chest,
for the face was turned round toward the back,
and they had to come backwards,
because seeing ahead was taken from them.
Perhaps by force of palsy, at some time,
someone has been twisted round so completely;
but I have not seen it, nor do I believe it happens.
So may God let you, reader, take fruit
from your reading, think now for yourself
who is more wicked than the one
who brings passion to the judgment of God?
Lift your head, lift it, and see the one for whom
the earth opened before the eyes of the Thebans,
so that they all shouted: ‘Where are you rushing,
Amphiaraus? Why are you leaving the war?’
And he did not stop plunging downward
as far as Minos, who lays hold of everyone.
See how he has made a breast of his shoulders;
because he wished to see too far ahead,
he looks behind and walks a backward road.
See Tiresias, who changed his appearance
when from male he became female,
all his limbs being changed, every one;
and afterwards he had first to strike again
the two entwined serpents with his rod
before he could have back his male plumage.
Aruns is the one who backs up to this one’s belly,
who in the mountains of Luni, where the soil is hoed
by the man of Carrara who lives below,
had a cave among the white marbles
for his dwelling, from which, for watching the stars
and the sea, his view was not cut off.
And she who covers her breasts,
which you do not see, with her loosened tresses,
and has on that side all her hairy skin,
was Manto, who searched through many lands;
then she settled where I was born;
and so it pleases me that you listen to me a little.
After her father had departed from life
and the city of Bacchus had become a slave,
she went about the world for a long time.
Up in fair Italy there lies a lake
at the foot of the Alps that shut in Germany
above Tyrol, and its name is Benaco.
By a thousand springs, I think, and more, [the land] is bathed
between Garda and Val Camonica and the Pennino
with the water that lies still in that lake.
There is a place in the middle where the Trentine
shepherd and the one of Brescia and the Veronese
could give a blessing, if he went that way.
Peschiera sits there, a fine strong fortress
for facing the Brescians and the Bergamasques,
where the shore round about is lowest.
There everything must spill over
that cannot stay in the lap of Benaco,
and becomes a river down through green pastures.
As soon as the water sets its head to running,
it is no longer called Benaco but Mincio,
as far as Governolo, where it falls into the Po.
It has not run far before it finds a low flat,
over which it spreads and turns it into marsh;
and in summer it is apt at times to be unwholesome.
Passing that way, the harsh virgin
saw land in the middle of the fen,
untilled and bare of inhabitants.
There, to flee all human company,
she stayed with her servants to practise her arts,
and lived, and left there her empty body.
Then the men who were scattered round about
gathered to that place, which was strong
because of the fen it had on every side.
They built the city over those dead bones;
and after her who first chose the place
they called it Mantua, with no other casting of lots.
Its people within were once more numerous,
before the folly of Casalodi
received deceit from Pinamonte.
So I instruct you that, if you ever hear
my city’s origin told otherwise,
you let no lie defraud the truth.”
And I: “Master, your accounts
are so certain to me, and so take hold of my belief,
if you see any of them worth noting;
for my mind turns back to that alone.”
Then he said to me: “That one who from his cheek
spreads his beard down over his dark shoulders
was — when Greece was so emptied of males
that they barely remained in the cradles —
an augur, and with Calchas he gave the moment
at Aulis for cutting the first cable.
Eurypylus was his name, and so he is sung
by my high tragedy in a certain place:
you know it well, who know the whole of it.
That other one, who is so slight in the flanks,
was Michael Scot, who truly
knew the game of magic frauds.
See Guido Bonatti; see Asdente,
who would like to have kept to his leather and his thread
now, but repents too late.
See the wretched women who left the needle,
the shuttle and the spindle, and made themselves fortune-tellers;
they worked spells with herbs and with images.
But come now, for already there holds the boundary
of both hemispheres, and touches the wave
and whom a sudden fear unmans,
so that, though looking, he does not delay his going:
and I saw behind us a black devil
come running up along the ridge.
Ah, how fierce he was in his look!
and how cruel he seemed to me in his bearing,
with his wings open and light upon his feet!
His shoulder, which was sharp and high,
a sinner loaded with both his haunches,
and he held him clutched by the sinews of the feet.
From our bridge he said: “O Malebranche,
here is one of the elders of Saint Zita!
Put him under, for I am going back for more
to that city, which is well stocked with them:
every man there is a grafter, except Bonturo;
there, for money, ‘no’ is made into ‘yes’.”
He flung him down there, and along the hard ridge
turned away; and never was a mastiff let loose
in such a hurry to pursue the thief.
That one sank under, and came back up doubled over;
but the demons who were sheltered by the bridge
cried: “Here the Holy Face has no place!
here one swims otherwise than in the Serchio!
So, if you want none of our clawing,
do not stick out above the pitch.”
Then they bit into him with more than a hundred hooks
and said: “Here you must dance under cover,
so that, if you can, you may snatch in secret.”
Not otherwise do cooks make their scullions
push down into the middle of the cauldron
the meat with their hooks, so that it does not float.
The good master: “So that it may not appear
that you are here,” he said to me, “crouch down
let one of you come forward to hear me,
and then take counsel about grappling me.”
They all cried: “Let Malacoda go!”
so one moved — and the others stood still —
and came to him saying: “What good will it do him?”
“Do you think, Malacoda, that you see me
come here,” said my master,
“already secure against all your defences,
without divine will and favourable fate?
Let us go on, for it is willed in heaven
that I show another this wild road.”
Then his pride was so fallen
that he let his hook drop at his feet,
and said to the others: “Now let him not be struck.”
And my leader to me: “O you who sit
among the splinters of the bridge, crouching low,
come back to me now in safety.”
So I moved and came quickly to him;
and the devils all pressed forward,
so that I doubted they would keep the pact;
so once I saw the foot soldiers afraid
who came out of Caprona under a truce,
seeing themselves among so many enemies.
I drew in with my whole body
close to my leader, and did not turn my eyes
from their looks, which were not good.
They lowered their hooks, and “Do you want me to touch him,”
one kept saying to another, “on the rump?”
And they answered: “Yes, see that you give it to him.”
But that demon who was holding talk
with my leader turned round very quickly
and said: “Easy, easy, Scarmiglione!”
Then he said to us: “To go further along this
ridge cannot be done, because there lies
all shattered at the bottom the sixth arch.
And if you still want to go forward,
go on up along this rocky bank;
close by is another ridge that makes a way.
Yesterday, five hours later than this hour,
one thousand two hundred and sixty-six
years were completed since the road here was broken.
I am sending some of these of mine over there
to see whether anyone is out airing himself;
go with them, for they will not do you harm.”
“Step forward, Alichino, and Calcabrina,”
he began to say, “and you, Cagnazzo;
and let Barbariccia lead the ten.
Let Libicocco come too, and Draghignazzo,
tusked Ciriatto and Graffiacane
and Farfarello and mad Rubicante.
Search around the boiling birdlime;
let these two be safe as far as the next crag
that runs all unbroken over the dens.”
“Oh me, master, what is this I see?”
I said, “please, let us go alone, without escort,
if you know the way; for I, for my part, do not ask for one.
If you are as watchful as you usually are,
do you not see that they are grinding their teeth
and threatening us with harm with their brows?”
And he to me: “I do not want you to be afraid;
let them grind away as they please,
for they do it at the boiled wretches.”
They wheeled round by the left-hand bank;
but first each had pressed his tongue
between his teeth toward their leader as a signal;
and he had made a trumpet of his arse.
I have seen horsemen before now break camp,
and begin an assault, and hold their muster,
not the one who fell from the walls at Thebes.
He fled away and spoke not one word more;
and I saw a centaur full of rage
come calling: "Where is he, where is the harsh one?"
I do not think the Maremma has as many
snakes as he had along his haunches
up to where our form begins.
On his shoulders, behind the nape,
a dragon lay on him with open wings;
and it sets on fire whoever it runs into.
My master said: "This is Cacus,
who, under the rock of Mount Aventine,
many a time made a lake of blood.
He does not go on one road with his brothers,
because of the theft he made by fraud
of the great herd that he had near him;
for which his crooked works came to an end
under the club of Hercules, who perhaps
gave him a hundred [blows], and he did not feel ten."
While he was speaking so, the other ran past,
and three spirits came below us,
one through the wound and the other through the mouth
smoked hard, and the smoke met.
Let Lucan now be silent where he touches
on wretched Sabellus and on Nasidius,
and wait to hear what is now let fly.
Let Ovid be silent about Cadmus and Arethusa,
for if he turns the one into a serpent and the other into a spring
in his poetry, I do not envy him;
for two natures face to face he never
transmuted so that both forms
were ready to exchange their matter.
They answered each other by such rules
that the serpent split its tail into a fork,
I am more certain; but I had already judged
that it was so, and already wanted to ask you:
who is in that fire that comes so divided
at the top that it seems to rise from the pyre
where Eteocles was laid with his brother?"
He answered me: "In there are tormented
Ulysses and Diomedes, and so together
they go to vengeance as they went to wrath;
and inside their flame they groan for
the ambush of the horse that made the gate
through which the noble seed of the Romans went out.
In it they weep for the craft for which, though dead,
Deidamia still grieves for Achilles,
and there they pay the penalty for the Palladium."
"If they can, inside those sparks,
speak," I said, "master, I pray you earnestly
then, moving its tip this way and that,
as if it were the tongue that spoke,
it cast a voice out and said: "When
I parted from Circe, who kept me
away for more than a year there, near Gaeta,
before Aeneas had given it that name,
neither the sweetness of a son, nor the reverence
for my old father, nor the love I owed
that should have made Penelope glad,
could overcome within me the ardour
I had to become expert in the world
and in the vices of men, and in their worth;
but I put out on the deep, open sea
with one ship only, and with that small
company by which I had not been deserted.
The one shore and the other I saw, as far as Spain,
as far as Morocco, and the island of the Sardinians,
and the others which that sea washes round.
My companions and I were old and slow
when we came to that narrow mouth
where Hercules set up his markers
so that no one should venture beyond;
on the right hand I left Seville behind,
on the other I had already left Ceuta.
'O brothers,' I said, 'who through a hundred thousand
dangers have reached the west,
to this so very brief watch
of our senses that remains to us
do not refuse the experience,
following the sun, of the world without people.
Consider the seed you sprang from:
you were not made to live like beasts,
but to pursue virtue and knowledge.'
I made my companions so keen,
with this little speech, for the voyage,
that afterwards I could hardly have held them back;
and, turning our stern toward the morning,
we made wings of our oars for the mad flight,
always gaining on the left-hand side.
All the stars of the other pole
the night now saw, and ours so low
that it did not rise out of the plain of the sea.
Five times rekindled and as many quenched
had been the light beneath the moon
since we had entered on the deep passage,
when a mountain appeared to us, dark
with distance, and it seemed to me so high
as I had never seen any.
We rejoiced, and soon it turned to weeping;
for from the new land a whirlwind rose
and struck the ship at its forward corner.
Three times it spun it round with all the waters;
at the fourth it lifted the stern up high
and sent the prow down, as pleased another,
until the sea had closed above us again."
The flame now stood upright and still,
having no more to say, and was already going away from us
long promising with short keeping
will make you triumph on the high throne.’
Francis came afterwards, when I had died,
for me; but one of the black cherubim
said to him: ‘Do not take him; do not wrong me.
He must come down among my wretches
because he gave the fraudulent counsel,
since which time I have been at his hair;
for one who does not repent cannot be absolved,
nor can one repent and will at the same time,
because of the contradiction, which does not allow it.’
Oh, wretched me! How I shuddered
when he seized me, saying to me: ‘Perhaps
you did not think I was a logician!’
He carried me to Minos; and he wrapped
his tail eight times around his hard back,
and after he had bitten it in his great rage,
said: ‘This is one of the sinners for the thieving fire’;
so I am lost there where you see me,
and, clothed like this, I go grieving.”
do not let your foul and loathsome punishment
frighten you from making yourselves known to me."
"I was from Arezzo, and Albero of Siena,"
one of them answered, "had me put to the fire;
but what I died for does not bring me here.
It is true that I said to him, speaking in jest,
'I would know how to lift myself through the air in flight';
and he, who had curiosity and little sense,
wanted me to show him the art; and only
because I did not make him Daedalus, he had me
burned by one who held him as a son.
But to the last ditch of the ten
I, for the alchemy I practised in the world,
was condemned by Minos, who is not permitted to err."
And I said to the poet: "Now, was there ever
a people as vain as the Sienese?
against the Sienese, sharpen your eye toward me,
so that my face may answer you clearly:
so you will see I am the shade of Capocchio,
who falsified metals with alchemy;
and you must remember, if I eye you rightly,
how good an ape of nature I was."
In the time when Juno was angered
because of Semele against the blood of Thebes,
so that it coloured both my cheeks,
and then held out the remedy to me;
so, I hear, the lance of Achilles
and of his father used to be the cause
first of a sad and then of a good gift.
We turned our backs on the wretched valley,
up over the bank that girds it all around,
which, as I followed its path back the way it came,
drew my eyes wholly to one place.
After the grievous rout, when
Charlemagne lost the holy company,
Roland did not sound [his horn] so terribly.
Not long had I held my head turned that way
when I seemed to see many high towers;
drawing nearer and nearer toward the edge,
my error fled from me and my fear grew;
for, just as on its round ring of walls
Montereggioni crowns itself with towers,
so the brink that surrounds the pit
for I saw thirty great spans of him
down from the place where a man buckles his cloak.
“Raphèl maì amècche zabì almi,”
the savage mouth began to cry,
for which no sweeter psalms were fitting.
And my leader toward him: “Foolish soul,
and see it, which hoops your great chest.”
Then he said to me: “He accuses himself;
this is Nimrod, through whose evil thought
a single language is no longer used in the world.
Let us leave him be, and not speak in vain;
for to him every language is just as
from the neck down, so that on the exposed part
it wound around him as far as the fifth turn.
“This proud one wanted to make trial
of his power against highest Jove,”
said my leader, “and so he has this reward.
Ephialtes is his name, and he did the great deeds
when the giants made the gods afraid;
the arms he plied he never moves again.”
And I to him: “If it can be, I would like
that of the immeasurable Briareus
and nothing more than the fear was needed,
had I not seen the bonds.
We went on further then,
and came to Antaeus, who a good five ells,
not counting the head, rose out of the pit.
"O you who, in the fortunate valley
that made Scipio heir to glory
when Hannibal and his men turned their backs,
once took a thousand lions as prey,
and of whom, had you been at the high war
of your brothers, it seems some still believe
the sons of the earth would have won:
set us down, and do not disdain to do it,
where the cold locks up Cocytus.
Do not make us go to Tityus or to Typhon:
this man can give some of what is longed for here;
whose throat Florence sawed through.
Gianni de' Soldanieri, I believe, is
further on, with Ganelon and Tebaldello,
who opened Faenza while it slept.”
We had already left him
And so that you may more willingly scrape
the glazed tears from my face,
know that as soon as the soul betrays,
as I did, its body is taken from it
by a demon, who governs it from then on
until its time has all run round.
It falls headlong into such a cistern as this;
and perhaps the body still appears up above
of the shade that winters here behind me.
You must know him, if you are only now coming down:
he is ser Branca Doria, and many years
have passed since he was shut up like this.”
“I believe,” I said to him, “that you are deceiving me;
for Branca Doria has never died,
and he eats and drinks and sleeps and puts on clothes.”
“In the ditch above,” he said, “of the Malebranche,
there where the sticky pitch boils,
Michel Zanche had not yet arrived
when this one left a devil in his place
in his own body, and [so did] a kinsman of his
who did the treachery together with him.
But now stretch out your hand here;
open my eyes.” And I did not open them for him;
then, because of the wind, I drew back behind
my leader, for there was no other shelter there.
I was now — and with fear I put it into verse —
where the shades were wholly covered,
and showed through like straw in glass.
Some are lying down; others stand upright,
this one on its head and that one on its soles;
another, like a bow, bends its face back to its feet.
When we had gone so far forward
that it pleased my master to show me
the creature that once had the fair countenance,
he moved from in front of me and made me stop,
“Here is Dis,” he said, “and here is the place
where you must arm yourself with fortitude.”
How frozen and faint I then became,
do not ask, reader, for I do not write it,
since any speech would fall short.
I did not die, and I did not stay alive;
think now for yourself, if you have a shred of wit,
what I became, deprived of both the one and the other.
The emperor of the sorrowful kingdom
rose out of the ice from the middle of his breast;
and I compare better with a giant
than the giants do with his arms:
see now how great that whole must be
that would be in proportion to such a part.
If he was once as fair as he is now foul,
and raised his brows against his maker,
well may all grief proceed from him.
Oh, how great a marvel it seemed to me
when I saw three faces on his head!
One in front, and that was vermilion;
the others were two, which joined this one
just above the middle of each shoulder,
and met each other at the place of the crest;
and the right one seemed between white and yellow;
the left was, to look at, like those
who come from where the Nile runs down into its valley.
Beneath each there came out two great wings,
of a size befitting so great a bird:
sails at sea I never saw like them.
They had no feathers, but like a bat’s
was their fashion; and he was flapping them,
so that three winds went out from him:
by these all Cocytus was frozen.
With six eyes he wept, and over three chins
dripped the tears and bloody drool.
In each mouth he was crushing with his teeth
a sinner, as a flax-brake does,
so that he kept three of them in pain like this.
To the one in front the biting was nothing
compared with the clawing, for at times his back
was left all stripped of skin.
“That soul up there who has the greatest punishment,”
said the master, “is Judas Iscariot,
who has his head inside and kicks his legs outside.
Of the other two, who have their heads below,
the one who hangs from the black snout is Brutus:
see how he writhes, and says not a word!
and the other is Cassius, who looks so thick-limbed.
But night is rising again, and now
it is time to leave, for we have seen everything.”
As he wished, I clasped him round the neck;
and he chose his moment and his place,
and when the wings were opened wide enough,
he took hold of the shaggy sides;
from tuft to tuft he then climbed down
between the thick hair and the frozen crusts.
When we had come to where the thigh
turns, just at the thick of the haunches,
my leader, with toil and with anguish,
turned his head to where he had had his shanks,
and grappled on the hair like a man who climbs,
so that I thought we were going back into hell.
“Hold on tight, for by such stairs,”
said the master, panting like a man worn out,
“we must depart from so much evil.”
Then he came out through an opening in a rock
and set me down on its edge to sit;
then he stretched his wary step toward me.
I raised my eyes and thought to see
Lucifer as I had left him,
and I saw him holding his legs upward;
and if I was troubled then,
let the dull-witted judge, who do not see
what that point is which I had passed.
“Get up,” said the master, “on your feet:
the way is long and the road is hard,
and already the sun is returning to mid-tierce.”
It was no palace hall
where we were, but a natural dungeon
that had a bad floor and a want of light.
“Before I tear myself away from the abyss,
my master,” I said when I was upright,
“talk to me a little, to draw me out of error:
where is the ice? and how is this one fixed
so upside down? and how, in so short a time,
has the sun made its passage from evening to morning?”
And he to me: “You imagine still
that you are on the far side of the centre, where I took hold
of the hair of the wicked worm that bores through the world.
You were on that side as long as I was descending;
when I turned myself, you passed the point
to which weights are drawn from every side.
And you have now come beneath the hemisphere
which is opposite to the one the great dry land
covers, and beneath whose summit was put to death
the man who was born and lived without sin;
you have your feet upon a little sphere
which forms the other face of the Judecca.
Here it is morning when there it is evening;
and this one, who made a ladder for us of his hair,
is still fixed just as he was before.
On this side he fell down from heaven;
and the land, which once stood out on this side,
for fear of him made a veil of the sea
and came to our hemisphere; and perhaps,
to flee from him, there left an empty space here
the [land] that appears on this side, and rushed upward.”
